english.notes:
(i) R v Hoof 1980 held that when dealing with an individual for reckless endangerment where fire is involved the offences of (a) intent to endanger life and; (b) recklessness whether life endangered should be charged separately. This would enable the trial judge, where the jury convict on (a) above, to discharge the jury from giving a verdict on (b).
(ii) Consent of the Director of Public Prosecutions is required where the damage is to a spouse's property (section 30(4) of the Theft Act 1968).
(iii) Property damaged or destroyed may belong to defendant.
(iv) The same incident may involve separate activities, some causing ordinary damage and some damage by fire (for example, protestors break into a laboratory building, smash laboratory equipment and set fire to some files). In such circumstances they are separate offences and best charged as such (R v Booth 1999).
